learn.title: A shortcut for remainders
learn.body: Dividing $P(x)$ by $x-a$ leaves a remainder, and the Remainder Theorem says it equals $P(a)$. No long division needed: just substitute $a$ into the polynomial.

learn.title: The Factor Theorem
learn.body: If the remainder is 0, the division is exact. So $x-a$ is a factor of $P(x)$ exactly when $P(a)=0$. This turns factor hunting into substitution: test a value, and if you get 0, you have found a factor.
For a factor like $x+2$, rewrite it as $x-(-2)$ and test $a=-2$. The sign flips.

questions.prompt: Find the remainder when $x^2+3x+1$ is divided by $x-2$.
What is the remainder of $x^3-2x+5$ divided by $x+1$?
$x-a$ is a factor of $P(x)$ exactly when $P(a)=\_\_$
questions.explanation: A zero remainder means the division is exact, so $x-a$ is a factor.
$P(1)=1-2-5+6=0$. For $x+1$ the value is $P(-1)=8$, and for $x-2$ it is $P(2)=-4$.

questions.prompt: For what value of $k$ is $x-2$ a factor of $x^3+kx-10$?
$P(x)=2x^2-5x+3$ and $P(1)=0$. What is the other factor besides $x-1$?

questions.explanation: Test $a=-3$: $(-3)^3+27=0$. The sign of $a$ is opposite to the sign in the factor.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for testing a factor in order.
questions.explanation: The test is substitution: a zero result means a factor.
